title: How America Cleared Forests Before Bulldozers
fullText: When the first European settlers stepped off their ships and walked inland, they did not see a country. They saw a wall. A wall of green that stretched from the Atlantic coast all the way past the Mississippi River, broken only by rivers and the occasional clearing left behind by Native Americans. Trees so wide that three men [music] could not link arms around the trunk. Trees so tall they blotted out the sun for hours of [music] the day. and underneath it all, a tangle of roots and undergrowth that swallowed sound and light alike. Over the next three centuries, Americans would clear more than 400 million acres of that forest using nothing but hand tools, animals, and fire, no bulldozers, no chainsaws, no hydraulic anything. Just axes, oxen, gunpowder, and the strongest backs in human history. And the methods they used killed more men than the wars of their time. This is how they did it. To understand the scale of what these settlers were facing, you have to forget every forest you have ever seen. The eastern forest in 1700 was something else entirely. White pines towering more than 200 ft into the sky. Tulip [music] poppplers with trunks as wide as a kitchen table. oaks that had been growing since before the Mayflower landed. The first colonists in places like Plymouth and [music] Jamestown described the forest as a kind of dim, cool cathedral where the canopy was so thick that grass could not [music] grow on the floor and it was not empty. Native Americans had been managing portions of the eastern woodlands for thousands of years, using controlled burns to keep undergrowth low and to encourage game [music] animals to come closer. But once those communities were displaced or destroyed by [music] disease and conflict, the forest closed back in. By the time waves of new settlers began pushing inland in the 1700s, they found themselves staring at an unbroken green ocean. And every single acre of farmland they wanted, they had to take from that ocean [music] tree by tree. The first weapon in this long war was the axe. Specifically, the American felling axe. European settlers had brought [music] their own axes with them, but they quickly discovered that the European designs were not suited to American hardwoods. So, American blacksmiths [music] got to work and over a few generations, they developed a heavier, broader, deadlier ax head that became one of the most important tools in the country's history. A skilled chopper could fell a tree 2 ft thick in under [music] 30 minutes using one of these axes. Some claimed even faster times in chopping [music] competitions. The records of frontier lumber camps describe men [music] who could drop a 100 trees in a single day. Now imagine doing that for 40 years. [music] Imagine your hands. Imagine your shoulders. Now imagine your hands. The average homestead family [music] of the 1800s would wear out somewhere between 10 and 20 axes across a single generation, sharpening them down to nubs [music] before grinding them away completely. And every settler boy learned to handle [music] one before he learned to read. But chopping a tree down was the easy part. The real [music] nightmare came after. Once a tree was on the ground, what then? [music] You had a massive log, sometimes weighing several tons, lying in the middle of where you wanted to plant corn. You had a stump [music] in the ground with roots reaching 10 ft down into the soil. You had a tangle [music] of branches and leaves called slash piled up around it. And you had to deal with all of [music] it before you could put a plow in the dirt. So, early settlers came up with [music] a shortcut. It was called girdling. Girdling was the lazy man's clearing method. Instead of cutting the whole tree down, you simply chopped a [music] deep ring all the way around the trunk, severing the layer of living wood that carried water from the roots to the leaves. The tree would die standing up, lose its leaves over the next year, and let sunlight reach the ground below. You could plant your first crops between the dead trees while you waited for them to slowly fall apart on their own. It was clever, it was efficient, and it was extremely dangerous. Because dead branches and rotting [music] limbs would drop without warning onto whoever happened to be plowing or planting underneath them, frontier doctors recorded so many deaths from falling timber that the woods themselves earned the nickname [music] widow makers. Hundreds of men died every year just from the trees [music] they had already killed. Even after the trees came down, the work was not finished. Now you had a field full of debris and the only way to deal with it was [music] fire. Burning the slash was a frontier ritual. Once a section of forest was felled, settlers would wait for a dry stretch of weather, pile the branches and unwanted timber into [music] massive heaps and set them ablaze. The smoke from these clearing fires hung over the eastern half of the country for entire seasons. Travelers in the 1800s described riding through valleys where the air was thick and orange for weeks at a time. Most of the time, these fires [music] stayed under control, but sometimes they did not. The most catastrophic [music] example happened on a single night in October of 1871 in a small Wisconsin lumber town [music] called Peshigo. A slash fire jumped its boundaries and swept across more than a million acres of cut over forest driven by hurricane force winds. The firestorm consumed the town in minutes. Witnesses [music] described tornadoes of flame, glass melting in windows, and people leaping into the river to escape only to be boiled alive. By morning, more than 1,500 people [music] were dead. It happened on the exact same night as the Great Chicago Fire. But because Pestigo was small [music] and remote, almost no one outside Wisconsin remembers it today. And it was just one of many [music] fires that came directly from the work of clearing land. But even with all the chopping, all the burning, and all the dying, the real enemy of the frontier farmer was still waiting in the ground, the stump. If you have never tried to remove [music] a tree stump by hand, you cannot understand what early American farmers were [music] up against. A mature oak stump could anchor itself 10 ft into the soil with roots reaching out 20 ft in every direction. The wood was dense, wet, and full of grit [music] that would dull any blade you tried to chop with, and there might be hundreds of them per acre. The simplest solution was to wait. Settlers would plow around [music] their stumps for years, sometimes a full decade, until the wood rotted [music] enough to be pulled out by hand or by oxen. You can still find old paintings and photographs of frontier fields full of [music] weathered black stumps poking up between rows of corn. Some farms in New England [music] carried their stumps for two generations before the land was finally clean. Others tried to speed things up. Stump pulling machines began appearing in the 1840s and50s. These were enormous wooden frames with iron [music] screws and chains powered by teams of oxen walking in slow circles. You would chain the device [music] to a stump, hit your oxen to a long pole, and start them walking. Slowly, agonizingly, the screw would lift, [music] and the roots would tear from the earth. It could take half a day to remove a single big stump, but it was faster than waiting 10 years. If you are still watching, hit that subscribe button and consider liking the video. It helps me keep digging up these forgotten [music] chapters of American history. Now, let's talk about the animals that did most of the actual [music] work. When you picture the American frontier, you probably picture horses. But on the homestead, horses were the second choice. The real engines of land clearing were oxen. A pair of working oxmen could pull 6,000 lb of dead weight day in and day out on minimal feed. They were slower than horses, but they were stronger, calmer, and far less likely to panic when a [music] chain snapped or a stump suddenly tore free of the ground. They could also live [music] on rough pasture and brush, which was exactly what a half-cleared farm [music] had in abundance. Skilled ox drivers, called teamsters, were respected men in frontier [music] communities. The job required patience, voice control, and a kind of low conversation with [music] the animals that took years to learn. The driver walked beside the team, never behind them, calling commands like G for right and for left with a long stick to guide [music] rather than strike. A good team of oxmen and a good driver could tear out roots, drag logs, [music] level hillsides, and break sod on land that no plow had ever touched. They were the muscle behind nearly every [music] clearing operation in the country until the late 1800s. And many of those animals were born, worked, and died on the same 160 acre farm that they had helped to carve out of [music] the forest. But oxen had their limits, and sometimes for the worst stumps and the hardest land, [music] you needed something more aggressive, you needed explosives. The use of gunpowder and later [music] dynamite for stump removal is one of the strangest chapters in American agricultural history. As early as the 1700s, [music] farmers were drilling deep holes into stumps with hand orers, packing them with black powder, plugging the hole with clay, and lighting a fuse. The result was dramatic. A wellplaced charge could shatter a stump completely, sending chunks of wood 30 ft into the air and leaving a crater in the soil that just needed to be filled in. After Alfred Nobel patented dynamite in 1867, the technology made its way to American farms within a few years. By the late 1800s, mail order cataloges like Sears Robuck were selling sticks of dynamite, blasting caps, and fuse cord directly to rural customers [music] alongside seeds, plows, and kitchen tools. Whole pamphlets were printed by [music] chemical companies explaining how a homesteader could blast stumps, blast ditches, even blast tree roots out of orchards. Accidents [music] were constant. A stick of dynamite that froze in a barn over the winter became dangerously unstable. A miscalculated charge could send wood through a barn wall, but the [music] trade-off was worth it. A single stick of dynamite could do in 5 seconds what a pair of oxen and a stump puller would need an entire day [music] to accomplish. By 1900, American farmers were using more [music] explosive material per year for clearing land than the United States Army was using for training. And by then, the federal government had already poured fuel on the fire of clearing with one of the largest land giveaways in human history. That giveaway was the Homestead Act of 1862. The law was simple. Any adult head of household who was a citizen or who intended to become one could claim60 [music] acres of public land for free. There was just one condition. They had to live on the land for 5 years, build a dwelling, and improve [music] it. And improvement in the language of the law almost always meant clearing trees and breaking soil. Over the next several decades, more than 270 million acres were claimed under the Homestead Act [music] and its later expansions. That is about 10% of the entire United States. 10% of [music] the country transferred from federal hands into private hands on the condition [music] that the new owners chopped down whatever forest stood in their way. And they did. Families poured [music] west out of New England, out of Pennsylvania, out of the Carolas, into Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Wisconsin, [music] and beyond, swinging axes and pulling stumps for years to keep their claim. The pace of forest clearing tripled in the decades after the Civil War, and the effects of that single law are still visible today. If you fly over the American Midwest, the perfect grid [music] of square farms below you was carved out almost entirely by hand in just two [music] generations. But while the homesteaders were busy clearing land for crops, an even bigger force was about to [music] reshape the forests of America. And it was not interested in farming. It was interested in profit. The rise of industrial logging in the late 1800s turned forest clearing into a national business. The white pine forests of Michigan, [music] Wisconsin, and Minnesota became the target. These three states alone supplied most of the lumber that built Chicago, St. Louis, and the rapidly growing cities of the Great Plains. The scale was staggering. Within just 40 years, between roughly 1860 and 1900, the great northern pine forests went from seemingly endless to almost completely gone. The technology that made [music] this possible was steam power. Lumber companies brought in steam powered skids, machines that use drums and cables to drag logs [music] out of the forest faster than any team of oxen could ever manage. On the West Coast in the Redwood and Douglas [music] fur country, an even more brutal device emerged. It was called the [music] Steam Donkey. The steam donkey was a small steam engine mounted on a wooden sled with a heavy cable wound around a winch drum. Loggers anchored it to a tree, ran the cable hundreds of feet into the forest, hooked it to a fallen log, [music] and let the engine drag the log back through the underbrush at terrifying speed. The steam donkey could move logs that weighed 30 tons or more. It tore the forest floor apart as it worked. Stumps, [music] soil, smaller trees, all dragged into the open. By the early 1900s, the steam donkey had replaced oxen across [music] most large logging operations on the Pacific coast. But the men who worked these operations paid a heavy price for the speed. The lumberjack camps of the late 1800s were some of the most dangerous workplaces in the country. Men signed on for entire [music] seasons, leaving home in the late fall and not returning until spring. They lived in long wooden bunk houses, dozens to a room, eating massive meals of pork, beans, bread, and coffee at long communal tables in silence because rules in most camps forbade talking during meals. The work began before sunrise [music] and ended after sundown. Temperatures often dropped well below zero. Frostbite, pneumonia, and tuberculosis [music] tore through the bunk houses every winter. But the real killers [music] were the trees themselves. A falling tree could snap a cable and whip a man in half. A rolling log could crush a leg or trap a foot. And worst of all, there was the so-called widow maker, the dead branch hanging in the canopy that could [music] drop without warning onto a logger's head as he was felling another tree below. Records from the largest lumber [music] states suggest that hundreds of loggers died every year throughout the late 18 hundreds in early 1900s. Many were buried where they fell. Some camps had their own cemeteries hidden in the woods marked only [music] by simple wooden crosses. But cutting the trees down was only the first step. Now the timber had to get to a sawmill. And in those days the answer was almost always water. The log drive is one of the most spectacular and forgotten parts of American history. After a winter of cutting, lumber companies would haul their logs onto frozen rivers and lakes. Stamp the ends with the company [music] brand and wait for the spring thor. When the ice broke, millions of logs would be released downstream, riding the high water all the way to the sawmills. To control the flow, loggers built temporary structures called splash dams. Wooden barriers that would back up a river into an artificial lake, then be opened all at once to send a flood of water [music] and timber rushing downstream. To keep the logs moving, men called river drivers walked, ran, [music] and even rode on top of the spinning logs as they tumbled through rapids and around bends. River drivers wore special boots called corks with sharp metal spikes on the soles that bit into the wet wood for grip. It is impossible to overstate how dangerous [music] this job was. Falling between two logs in a river drive almost always meant death. The logs would close together over your head [music] before anyone could reach you. Drivers drowned in cold spring rivers every single season. But the drives kept happening year after year because they were the only way to move that [music] much timber that fast. By the early 1900s, the consequences of all this clearing were becoming impossible to ignore. The eastern forest, which had once stretched in unbroken grandeur [music] from the Atlantic to the Mississippi, was largely gone. In its place stood farms, towns, and a patchwork of cut over land covered in [music] stumps and brush. Top soil that had been held in place for thousands of years by tree roots was now [music] washing off cleared hillsides every time it rained, choking rivers and clogging harbors. Floods became more violent because the forests that once absorbed rainfall were no longer there. Dust storms [music] began blowing through the great plains as the prairie sod was broken up. By 1900, conservationists [music] like Gford Pincho and Theodore Roosevelt began warning that America had clear-cut [music] itself into a coming disaster. The national forest system was created in part as a response. Reforestation efforts began in the eastern states. Today, if you walk through the woods of New England, of New York, of Pennsylvania, [music] you are mostly walking through second growth or third growth forest. The original cathedrals of timber are [music] long gone. Only a few scattered groves of ancient trees remain in places like the Cook forest of Pennsylvania or the old [music] growth pockets of the Smoky Mountains. And yet the work that those settlers and loggers did is [music] still everywhere around us, even if we have stopped seeing it. Here is a strange little fact. If you walk through almost any forest [music] in the eastern United States today, you will eventually run into a stone wall. A long low wall of stacked rocks [music] running through the trees, sometimes for miles. People sometimes assume these walls are old [music] property markers from some earlier century, which they are, but they miss the [music] bigger story. Those walls are evidence of fields. They mark the edges of farms that were cleared by hand, plowed for decades, and then abandoned when the family moved west or [music] quit farming. The forest grew back over the fields, but the walls remained. There are estimated to be more than 240,000 mi of stone walls in New England alone. Every single rock [music] in those walls was lifted by a human hand. Every single one. They mark a country that was carved out of the woods by axes and oxen and then partially returned to the [music] woods when the work was no longer worth it. Many of the family farms that still operate in places like Vermont, New Hampshire or upstate New York [music] were cleared from forest within the last 150 years. Some of them by people whose [music] grandchildren are still alive. The settlers who did this work did not have machines. They had time, muscle, and stubbornness. They lost fingers, eyes, and sometimes their lives. They watched their children grow up swinging the same axes they had used as boys. [music] They burned the woods. They blew up the stumps. They wore out the [music] oxen. And inch by inch, they turned a continent of trees into a continent of farms, towns, [music] and cities. That world we live in now, the open fields, the small towns, the patchwork [music] of farmland visible from any airplane window, was not built by bulldozers or chainsaws. [music] It was built by people who would never see those tools invented. People whose names are mostly [music] forgotten now, buried in country churchyards under stones that the weather has worn smooth. They cleared the [music] forest one tree at a time, one stump at a time, one season at [music] a time. And whatever you think of what they did, whether you see it as triumph or as tragedy [music] or as both, the scale of the labor is almost beyond modern understanding. 400 million acres of forest transformed [music] by hand in three centuries. The next time you drive through the countryside and see an old stone wall snaking off into the trees, slow down for [music] a second and look at it. Somebody put every single one of those rocks there. And somewhere nearby, [music] somebody also chopped down the tree that used to be standing right where you are looking with an axe by hand [music] and probably more than once.
